newsitem.title: USA: POLL--US June industrial output rose slightly.
newsitem.headline: POLL--US June industrial output rose slightly.

text.p: U.S. industrial production data would show that output edged up a bit in June after a moderate rise in May but utilized slightly less of the nation's production capacity, economists said.

The Federal Reserve's industrial production report, due at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT on Wednesday, was expected to show that U.S. output rose 0.2 percent in June after rising 0.4 percent in May. Capacity use -- the portion of the nation's factories, mines and utilities employed in that production -- was forecast to have eased to 83.6 from 83.7 percent.

"You have different forces pushing and pulling in different directions," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. Moran said a drop in the length of the average workweek in June, reported in the U.S. Labor Department's June employment report, boded poorly for manufacturing in June, as did figures showing only a slight increase in the number of new production workers hired in the manufacturing sector.
"Those figures told you that industrial production should be soft," he said.
On the other hand, the "unwinding" of the effects of spring auto strikes in June increased productivity in the auto sector and that should help to boost output, Moran said.
Capacity utilization could slip slightly, economists said, because of increased capacity and productivity.
"We've seen a strong, consistent trend of productivity growth in the manufacturing sector," said Moran.

Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Securities Inc, said industrial production and capacity use data might be overshadowed by the June Consumer Price Index (CPI) set to come out 45 minutes earlier.
"The CPI will be the headline grabber for the most part," said Flanagan. "Unless industrial production deviates a lot from the consensus, the figures at 0915 (EDT) will have a limited impact."
But other analysts said the market would want to set the industrial production data into a broader context of what it would mean for the economy later this year.

"People are really trying to figure out what is going to happen to growth and to Fed policy later in the year," said William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "So they want any number they can get -- either on the manufacturing side or on the consumer side of the economy -- to help them answer that question."
